---
title: "Case studies: reanalysis of published experiments"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

These case studies reanalyse six published experiments whose designs
differ in the number of stressors, in their levels and in the interactions
they identify, from a field experiment with two stressors to a full
factorial of five on split plots. Their data come with the package, reduced
to what the reanalyses use; the help page of each data set gives its
source, its licence and how it was prepared. Each section describes the
study and its design, how must models it and what it finds.
`vignette("must")` explains each step. The reanalyses illustrate the
package and do not replace those of the original articles; where their
conclusions differ, the section says why.

| Experiment | Stressors (levels) | Units and structure | Response | Contrast sets |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Alba et al. (2026) | drought, invasion (2 x 2) | 40 field plots in 10 blocks, 4 samplings | arthropod counts | 1 pair |
| Fuggle et al. (2025) | nutrients, salinity, in two orders | 18 ponds, 2 samplings | biofilm production | 1 pair per order |
| Giesler et al. (2023) | temperature (3), photoperiod (3), microbiome (2) | 48 wells per combination, 2 species | growth rate | 8 pairs and 4 triples per species |
| Vasquez et al. (2017) | temperature (4), salinity (3), oxygen (3) | embryos of 6 mating pairs | embryos developed | 16 pairs, 12 triples |
| Hunn et al. (2024) | CO2, heatwaves, sediment, flow (2^4^) | 128 stream mesocosms on 8 header tanks | invertebrate counts | 6 pairs, 4 triples, 1 of four |
| Niboyet et al. (2025) | CO2, warming, water, nitrogen, fire (2^5^) | 128 quadrants of 32 plots, 5 samplings | potential denitrification | 10 pairs, 10 triples, 5 of four, 1 of five |

In the six experiments the stressors act in different ways, none is a
toxicant that acts specifically on a physiological process, the responses
are not mortality, and no stressor has the levels needed to establish its
stressor-effect relationship. `suggest_null_models()` is therefore called
with the same criteria in every section. How the sensitivities of
individuals to the stressors are correlated is not known and is left
unknown, so that each of its values is tried; the guidelines of Schäfer &
Piggott (2018) then keep simple addition (AD), the multiplicative model (MU)
and dominance (DO), which is defined for pairs of stressors.

```{r setup}
library(must)
suggest <- function(fit) {
  suggest_null_models(fit, similar_action = FALSE, specific_action = FALSE,
                      mortality = FALSE, stressor_effect = FALSE)
}
```

The residual checks of `fit_responses()` are switched off
(`residual_checks = FALSE`) only so that these case studies run without the
DHARMa package; in an analysis, keep the default.

## Drought and plant invasion in a pine understory

Alba et al. (2026) asked how invasion by cogongrass (*Imperata
cylindrica*), a grass that forms dense stands where it has been introduced
in the southeastern United States, and drought change the arthropods of a
regenerating longleaf pine understory in Florida. Forty plots were planted
with pines and native plants in 2012; from spring 2013, rainout shelters
simulated drought, and cogongrass was planted in half of the plots.
Arthropods were collected with sweep nets in summer and fall of 2014 and
2015.

Each of ten blocks has one plot of each combination of the two stressors,
and every plot was sampled four times. `describe_design()` finds the
complete blocks, the repeated measures and the single contrast set:

```{r alba-design}
alba_design <- describe_design(alba_arthropods, stressors = c("drought", "invasion"),
                               control = c(drought = "ambient", invasion = "uninvaded"),
                               unit = "plot", time = "sampling", groups = "block")
alba_design
```

The analysis follows the total of the ten arthropod groups and the flies,
the group with the clearest interaction in the article. Both are counts,
and `fit_responses()` selects the negative binomial for both, with random
intercepts for the plot and the block; for the total, the block intercept
had a variance of zero and was removed.

```{r alba-fit}
alba_fit <- fit_responses(alba_arthropods, c("total", "flies"), alba_design,
                          residual_checks = FALSE, seed = 1, quiet = TRUE)
alba_fit
alba_est <- estimate_interactions(alba_fit, null_models = suggest(alba_fit), seed = 2026)
summary(alba_est)
e <- alba_est$estimates
# Effects of each stressor alone on the total, as multiples of the control
single <- e[e$response == "total" & e$component == "single" & e$null_model == "MU",
            c("time", "stressor", "estimate", "lower", "upper", "p_adjusted")]
single[c("estimate", "lower", "upper")] <- round(exp(single[c("estimate", "lower", "upper")]), 2)
single$p_adjusted <- signif(single$p_adjusted, 2)
single
# Deviations of the flies averaged over the samplings, relative to the control
flies <- e[e$response == "flies" & e$component == "interaction" & e$time == "overall",
           c("null_model", "relative", "p_value", "p_adjusted")]
flies[2:4] <- lapply(flies[2:4], signif, 2)
flies
```

```{r alba-numbers, include = FALSE}
invasion <- single[single$stressor == "invasion", ]
```

Invasion reduced the arthropods: averaged over the samplings, invaded plots
held `r invasion$estimate[invasion$time == "overall"]` times the total of
uninvaded ones, and `r invasion$estimate[invasion$time == "3"]` times in
summer 2015, two years after the invasion began. Drought alone had no
effect that the model can tell from zero. No deviation from any of the three
null models is significant for the total or for the flies once the p-values
are adjusted across the samplings, and every class of Piggott et al. (2015)
is AD. The article
reported a negative synergism of invasion and drought for the flies, from
Wald z tests, which assume infinite degrees of freedom, of a model with the
four-way interaction of the two stressors, season and year. Here the flies
deviate most from dominance, averaged over the samplings: fewer flies than
the more harmful stressor alone predicts, the direction of a negative
synergism, but with p = `r flies$p_value[flies$null_model == "DO"]`.

```{r alba-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.4}
plot(alba_est, type = "models", response = "flies", time = "overall")
```

## Salinisation and nutrient enrichment in two orders

Fuggle et al. (2025) asked whether the order in which two stressors arrive
changes their combined effect. Biofilms grown on ceramic tiles were moved to
outdoor ponds of 1000 L in central Spain, which received elevated salinity
(15 g NaCl/L), nutrients (nitrogen and phosphorus), both a week apart in
either order, or neither; ponds that received the same stressor twice form
no interaction and are left out. The gross primary production of the
biofilm was measured 1 and 21 days after the second application; on day 81
the pond water had become anoxic, and it was not measured.

The two orders are two interactions of the same stressors, and they share
their reference cells: the ambient ponds and those with a single stressor.
With the order as a `by` group and the shared ponds declared in `shared`,
`describe_design()` builds one contrast set per order, each completed by the
same ponds; without `shared`, neither order would have its control or its
single stressors, and nothing would be identifiable. The single stressors
were applied with the first application, so each order is compared with
ponds that had each stressor alone from the start.

```{r fuggle-design}
fuggle_design <- describe_design(fuggle_biofilms, stressors = c("nutrients", "salinity"),
                                 control = c(nutrients = "none", salinity = "none"),
                                 unit = "pond", time = "day", by = "sequence",
                                 shared = c(sequence = "single"))
fuggle_design$sets[, c("set_id", "sequence", "stressors", "net_identifiable", "shared")]
```

Gross production is continuous, with one sample at zero. `fit_responses()`
selects a Tweedie model, which allows exact zeros, with a log link and a
random intercept per pond; the samplings of day 81, without measurements,
are left out.

```{r fuggle-fit}
fuggle_fit <- fit_responses(fuggle_biofilms, "gross_production", fuggle_design,
                            residual_checks = FALSE, seed = 1, quiet = TRUE)
fuggle_fit
fuggle_est <- estimate_interactions(fuggle_fit, null_models = suggest(fuggle_fit), seed = 2025)
e <- fuggle_est$estimates
ad <- e[e$component == "interaction" & e$null_model == "AD",
        c("sequence", "time", "estimate", "lower", "upper", "p_value", "p_adjusted")]
ad[3:5] <- lapply(ad[3:5], round)
ad[6:7] <- lapply(ad[6:7], signif, 2)
ad
measured <- fuggle_biofilms[fuggle_biofilms$day < 81, ]
round(with(measured, tapply(gross_production, list(treatment, day), mean)))
```

```{r fuggle-numbers, include = FALSE}
means <- with(measured, tapply(gross_production, list(treatment, day), mean))
first <- ad[ad$sequence == "salinity first" & ad$time == "1", ]
ratio <- round(means["NS", "1"] / means["SN", "1"], 2)
```

```{r fuggle-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.6}
plot(fuggle_est, type = "interactions", group_by = "set")
```

Neither order deviates from any null model on either day. The largest
deviation is that of salinity first on day 1: gross production was
`r format(first$estimate, big.mark = ",")` units above the additive
expectation, about as much as the production of the controls, but with
three or four ponds per treatment its interval runs from
`r format(first$lower, big.mark = ",")` to
`r format(first$upper, big.mark = ",")` (p = `r first$p_value`). Because
the two orders share every other cell, the difference between their
interactions is the difference between the two sequences themselves. That
contrast is what the article reported: on day 1 the ponds that received
nutrients first produced `r ratio` times as much as those that received
salinity first. must does not test that contrast, because it compares two
treatments rather than a combination with its null model; a comparison of
treatments in the fitted model, such as those of the emmeans package, can.

## Temperature, photoperiod and the microbiome of two diatoms

Giesler et al. (2023) grew a polar diatom (*Thalassiosira gravida*) and a
temperate one (*T. rotula*) at three temperatures and three photoperiods,
with their microbiome or without it (axenic cultures), to ask whether the
light regime and the bacteria associated with a diatom shape its response
to temperature. The response is the maximum growth rate of each culture in
a well of a 96-well plate over a week.

Each species has 18 combinations with 48 wells each. The reference is the
culture condition of the polar diatom, 4 °C and 16 h of light, with the
microbiome; 16 h lies between the two other photoperiods, so a shorter and
a longer day are both departures from it. With the species as a `by` group,
each species has 8 pairs and 4 triples of stressor levels, each set with the
reference. The data identify neither the plates nor the climate cabinets,
so the wells count as independent units, as in the original analysis. The
wells of a combination shared its incubation, however, and the precision
of the estimates is that of wells, not of independent incubations.

```{r giesler-design}
giesler_design <- describe_design(giesler_diatoms,
                                  stressors = c("temperature", "photoperiod", "microbiome"),
                                  control = c(temperature = "4", photoperiod = "16",
                                              microbiome = "present"),
                                  by = "species")
table(giesler_design$sets$species, giesler_design$sets$order)
```

Growth rates can be negative (cultures that declined), so the model is
Gaussian with an identity link. Their variance differs widely among the
combinations. The article weighted each combination by the inverse of its
variance; `dispersion = "cell"` estimates one residual variance per
combination instead, and the degrees of freedom of each contrast then
follow the Welch-Satterthwaite approximation.

```{r giesler-fit}
giesler_common <- fit_responses(giesler_diatoms, "growth_rate", giesler_design,
                                residual_checks = FALSE, seed = 1, quiet = TRUE)
giesler_fit <- fit_responses(giesler_diatoms, "growth_rate", giesler_design,
                             dispersion = "cell", residual_checks = FALSE, seed = 1,
                             quiet = TRUE)
aic <- c(common = AIC(giesler_common$fits$growth_rate$model),
         cell = AIC(giesler_fit$fits$growth_rate$model))
round(aic)
giesler_est <- estimate_interactions(giesler_fit, null_models = suggest(giesler_fit),
                                     seed = 2023)
summary(giesler_est)
```

```{r giesler-microbiome}
e <- giesler_est$estimates
classes <- classify_interactions(giesler_est)
removal <- function(x) {
  x$null_model == "AD" & x$order == 2L &
    grepl("photoperiod=16 | microbiome=removed", x$levels, fixed = TRUE)
}
# Removing the microbiome at each temperature, with 16 h of light
lost <- merge(e[removal(e) & e$component == "interaction",
                c("species", "set_id", "levels", "observed", "expected", "p_adjusted")],
              classes[removal(classes), c("species", "set_id", "class")])
lost$levels <- sub(" \\|.*", "", lost$levels)
lost[c("observed", "expected")] <- lapply(lost[c("observed", "expected")], round, 2)
lost$p_adjusted <- signif(lost$p_adjusted, 2)
lost[, -2]
agreement <- compare_null_models(giesler_est)
table(agreement$species, agreement$agreement)
long_day <- e[e$component == "interaction" & e$species == "T. rotula" &
                e$levels == "temperature=13.5 | photoperiod=24 | microbiome=present",
              c("null_model", "observed", "expected")]
long_day[2:3] <- lapply(long_day[2:3], round, 2)
long_day
```

```{r giesler-numbers, include = FALSE}
counts <- function(model) {
  x <- e[e$component == "interaction" & e$estimand == "net" & e$null_model == model, ]
  c(deviating = sum(x$p_adjusted < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE), tested = sum(x$status == "ok"))
}
ad_counts <- counts("AD")
mu_counts <- counts("MU")
mean_rate <- function(species, temperature, microbiome) {
  x <- giesler_diatoms[giesler_diatoms$species == species & giesler_diatoms$photoperiod == 16 &
                         giesler_diatoms$temperature == temperature &
                         giesler_diatoms$microbiome == microbiome, ]
  round(mean(x$growth_rate), 2)
}
```

One variance per combination lowers the AIC by
`r round(aic[["common"]] - aic[["cell"]])` points. Almost every interaction
deviates: `r ad_counts[["deviating"]]` of the
`r ad_counts[["tested"]]` net deviations under AD, and
`r mu_counts[["deviating"]]` of the `r mu_counts[["tested"]]` that MU can
test (the others need cells whose mean growth is zero or negative). The two
species differ in direction. Removing the microbiome of the polar diatom
barely changed its growth at 4 °C
(`r mean_rate("T. gravida", 4, "present")` and
`r mean_rate("T. gravida", 4, "removed")` per day), but at 9 and 13.5 °C it
cut growth far below the additive expectation, a negative synergism (−S):
the microbiome sustained growth at the warm margin of the polar diatom. The
temperate diatom lost more than half of its growth without the microbiome
at 4 °C (`r mean_rate("T. rotula", 4, "present")` and
`r mean_rate("T. rotula", 4, "removed")`), the cold margin of its range,
and much less at warmer temperatures (−A). Other deviations depend on the
null model. At 13.5 °C and 24 h, *T. rotula* grew less than AD predicts and
more than MU and DO do: continuous light cut its growth to a quarter at 4 °C,
and that loss is subtracted under AD but scaled under MU, so the
observation falls between the two expectations and `compare_null_models()`
calls the deviation conflicting.

The sets that remove the microbiome at 9 and 13.5 °C, with 16 h of light,
under AD:

```{r giesler-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 8.5}
plot(giesler_est, set_id = unique(lost$set_id))
```

and the conflicting set of *T. rotula* under each null model:

```{r giesler-models, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.4}
conflict <- e$set_id[e$species == "T. rotula" & e$component == "interaction" &
                       e$levels == "temperature=13.5 | photoperiod=24 | microbiome=present"]
plot(giesler_est, type = "models", set_id = unique(conflict))
```

## Temperature, salinity and oxygen in horseshoe crab embryos

Horseshoe crabs (*Limulus polyphemus*) lay their eggs in beach sediment,
where the embryos can meet high temperatures, low salinity and low oxygen.
Vasquez et al. (2017) exposed eggs of six mating pairs from Delaware Bay to
each combination of four temperatures, three salinities and three oxygen
levels for two weeks, kept them for two more weeks in the reference
condition, and recorded which embryos reached the size of a late-stage
embryo (5 mm²); the article compared the results with those of an earlier
experiment on a population of the Gulf coast of Florida.

The 36 combinations form 16 pairs and 12 triples of non-reference levels,
each with the reference (30 °C, 34 ppt and 21% oxygen), which is not at the
end of the temperature gradient: 20 and 25 °C are colder than it and 35 °C
is warmer. Every mating pair contributed eggs to every combination, so the
pairs are complete blocks. Each combination occupied one plate, so plates
are confounded with combinations; as in the original analysis, the units
are the embryos of a pair in a combination.

```{r vasquez-design}
vasquez_design <- describe_design(vasquez_embryos,
                                  stressors = c("temperature", "salinity", "oxygen"),
                                  control = c(temperature = "30", salinity = "34",
                                              oxygen = "21"),
                                  groups = "pair")
vasquez_design
```

The response is the number of embryos that developed out of those measured,
given in `trials`. `fit_responses()` selects the beta-binomial, which allows
for more variation among units than the binomial, with a random intercept
per pair. Five combinations have no embryo developed at all; their means sit at
the boundary of the logit link, and the contrasts that need them are
treated apart.

```{r vasquez-fit}
vasquez_fit <- fit_responses(vasquez_embryos, "developed", vasquez_design,
                             trials = c(developed = "embryos"),
                             residual_checks = FALSE, seed = 1, quiet = TRUE)
vasquez_fit
vasquez_est <- estimate_interactions(vasquez_fit, null_models = suggest(vasquez_fit),
                                     seed = 2017)
summary(vasquez_est)
e <- vasquez_est$estimates
ad <- e[e$component == "interaction" & e$null_model == "AD", ]
table(ad$status, ad$estimand)
deviating <- ad[ad$status != "not_estimable" & ad$p_adjusted < 0.05,
                c("levels", "estimand", "observed", "expected", "p_adjusted", "status")]
deviating[c("observed", "expected")] <- lapply(deviating[c("observed", "expected")], round, 2)
deviating$p_adjusted <- signif(deviating$p_adjusted, 2)
deviating
```

```{r vasquez-numbers, include = FALSE}
developed <- function(temperature, salinity, oxygen) {
  x <- vasquez_embryos[vasquez_embryos$temperature == temperature &
                         vasquez_embryos$salinity == salinity & vasquez_embryos$oxygen == oxygen, ]
  paste(sum(x$developed), "of", sum(x$embryos))
}
not_estimable <- sum(ad$status == "not_estimable" & ad$estimand == "net")
```

Low salinity alone (5 ppt at 30 °C and 21% oxygen) stopped the development
of every embryo (`r developed(30, 5, 21)`). A combination with only zeros
can still be tested, from the probability of that outcome under the null
model, but a stressor alone with only zeros leaves no effect to combine, so
the `r not_estimable` sets that need that cell are not estimable, each with
its reason in `reason`. Of the others, two pairs deviate under every null
model, both negative synergisms. At 35 °C and 5% oxygen no embryo developed
(`r developed(35, 34, 5)`, a boundary test), although each stressor alone
left most of them developing (`r developed(35, 34, 21)` and
`r developed(30, 34, 5)`). At 35 °C and 15 ppt only
`r developed(35, 15, 21)` developed, against `r developed(35, 34, 21)` and
`r developed(30, 15, 21)` with each stressor alone. The pure interaction of
35 °C, 15 ppt and 13% oxygen is positive: mild hypoxia let most embryos
develop in warm brackish water (`r developed(35, 15, 13)`), far more than
the pairwise interactions predict.

A set that needs the cell with low salinity alone, and the two pairs that
deviate, under AD; triangles mark the tests from only zeros:

```{r vasquez-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 8}
deviating_sets <- unique(ad$set_id[which(ad$estimand == "net" & ad$p_adjusted < 0.05)])
needs_zeros <- ad$set_id[which(ad$estimand == "net" & ad$status == "not_estimable")][1]
plot(vasquez_est, set_id = c(needs_zeros, deviating_sets))
```

## Four stressors on header tanks

Hunn et al. (2024) combined two climate stressors, CO2 enrichment and
heatwaves, with fine sediment and variable flow in 128 outdoor stream
mesocosms in New Zealand, and counted the benthic invertebrates after seven
weeks. Their analysis found most interactions between CO2 and sediment:
copepods, for instance, doubled under CO2 without sediment and did not
respond to CO2 with it.

The full factorial of four stressors has eight mesocosms per combination,
in two blocks, and identifies 6 pairs, 4 triples and the interaction of all
four, with their pure interactions. The mesocosms, however, were fed by
eight header tanks, and temperature and CO2 were applied to the tanks: each
tank carried one combination of the two, and each combination two tanks.
`hunn_invertebrates` adds the tanks, deduced from the channel numbers (see
`?hunn_invertebrates`). Given as a group, they are found to be whole units
for temperature and CO2, replicated twice per combination of their levels:

```{r hunn-design}
hunn_stressors <- c("temperature", "co2", "sediment", "flow")
hunn_control <- c(temperature = "ambient", co2 = "ambient", sediment = "none",
                  flow = "constant")
hunn_design <- describe_design(hunn_invertebrates, hunn_stressors, hunn_control,
                               unit = "channel", groups = c("block", "header_tank"))
hunn_design$groups[, c("group", "n_groups", "between", "structure", "groups_per_combination")]
```

Copepods are counts, modelled with a negative binomial and a random
intercept per tank. The total abundance counts annelid fragments as halves,
so it is continuous, and a lognormal model fits it best. For every set that
involves temperature or CO2, the degrees of freedom are those of the tanks:
8 tanks, minus the 4 combinations of the two stressors and 1 for the second
block, leave 3. Only the set of sediment and flow, which vary within the
tanks, keeps 108. For interactions between a stressor of the tanks and one
of the mesocosms, such as CO2 and sediment, which vary partly within the
tanks, that rule is conservative (see `?estimate_interactions`).

```{r hunn-fit}
hunn_fit <- fit_responses(hunn_invertebrates, c("copepoda", "total_abundance"), hunn_design,
                          residual_checks = FALSE, seed = 1, quiet = TRUE)
hunn_fit
hunn_est <- estimate_interactions(hunn_fit, null_models = suggest(hunn_fit), seed = 2024)
summary(hunn_est)
e <- hunn_est$estimates
unique(e[e$component == "interaction" & e$estimand == "net", c("stressors", "df")])
```

```{r hunn-copepods}
round(with(hunn_invertebrates, tapply(copepoda, list(co2, sediment), mean)), 1)
co2_sediment <- function(est) {
  x <- est$estimates
  x <- x[x$response == "copepoda" & x$component == "interaction" &
           x$stressors == "co2 x sediment",
         c("null_model", "observed", "expected", "df", "p_value", "p_adjusted")]
  x[2:3] <- lapply(x[2:3], round, 1)
  x[5:6] <- lapply(x[5:6], signif, 2)
  x
}
co2_sediment(hunn_est)
# The same analysis with the mesocosms as independent replicates, as in the article
channels <- describe_design(hunn_invertebrates, hunn_stressors, hunn_control,
                            unit = "channel", groups = "block")
channels_fit <- fit_responses(hunn_invertebrates, "copepoda", channels,
                              residual_checks = FALSE, seed = 1, quiet = TRUE)
channels_est <- estimate_interactions(channels_fit, null_models = suggest(channels_fit),
                                      seed = 2024)
co2_sediment(channels_est)
```

```{r hunn-numbers, include = FALSE}
tanks <- co2_sediment(hunn_est)
alone <- co2_sediment(channels_est)
```

No interaction deviates from any null model for either response once the
p-values are adjusted across the 11 sets. The copepods show the pattern of
the article, and their deviation of CO2 and sediment from AD is negative:
with both stressors there were fewer copepods than the sum of their single
effects predicts. With the tanks as the replicates of CO2, its p-value is
`r tanks$p_value[tanks$null_model == "AD"]`. With the mesocosms as
independent replicates, as in the article, the same deviation has 111
degrees of freedom and p = `r alone$p_value[alone$null_model == "AD"]`,
which the adjustment across the 11 sets raises to
`r alone$p_adjusted[alone$null_model == "AD"]`. The four-stressor design
identifies every interaction, but for those that involve temperature or CO2
its replication is that of two tanks per combination. On a common axis, the
copepods under CO2 and sediment with the tanks, and with the mesocosms, as
the replicates of CO2:

```{r hunn-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4, fig.show = "hold"}
co2 <- unique(e$set_id[e$stressors == "co2 x sediment"])
both <- rbind(hunn_est$estimates, channels_est$estimates)
both <- both[both$response == "copepoda" & both$set_id == co2 & both$null_model == "AD", ]
xlim <- grDevices::extendrange(c(0, both$lower, both$upper), f = 0.05)
plot(hunn_est, response = "copepoda", set_id = co2, xlim = xlim,
     main = "Header tanks as the replicates of CO2")
plot(channels_est, set_id = co2, xlim = xlim, main = "Mesocosms as independent replicates")
```

## Five global changes on split plots

The Jasper Ridge Global Change Experiment has applied elevated CO2,
warming, increased precipitation and nitrogen addition to an annual
grassland in California since 1998, and a controlled fire burned half of
its plots in 2011. Niboyet et al. (2025) measured potential denitrification
(the activity of denitrifying enzymes in the soil) two days after the fire
and 5, 9, 21 and 33 months later. The combined effects departed from
additive, multiplicative and dominance expectations: positively when the
soil was wet, negatively when it was dry, and more the more global changes
were combined.

CO2, warming and fire were applied to 32 plots in four blocks, and
precipitation and nitrogen to the four quadrants of each plot. The full
factorial of five stressors identifies 26 contrast sets: 10 pairs, 10
triples, 5 sets of four and the set of all five, each with its pure
interaction from three stressors on. `describe_design()` finds the complete
blocks and the plots as whole units, and asks whether month 0 is a
baseline. It is not: it was sampled two days after the fire and thirteen
years after the other treatments began.

```{r niboyet-design}
niboyet_design <- describe_design(niboyet_denitrification,
                                  stressors = c("co2", "temperature", "water", "nitrogen",
                                                "fire"),
                                  control = c(co2 = "ambient", temperature = "ambient",
                                              water = "ambient", nitrogen = "ambient",
                                              fire = "unburned"),
                                  unit = "unit", time = "months", groups = c("block", "plot"))
niboyet_design
```

Potential denitrification is positive and continuous: a Gamma model with a
log link fits it, with random intercepts for the blocks, the plots and the
quadrants, which were sampled five times. The sets with a stressor of the
plots have 21 degrees of freedom (32 plots, minus 8 combinations of CO2,
warming and fire, minus 3 for the blocks); the set of water and nitrogen,
72.

```{r niboyet-fit}
niboyet_fit <- fit_responses(niboyet_denitrification, "denitrification", niboyet_design,
                             residual_checks = FALSE, seed = 1, quiet = TRUE)
niboyet_fit
niboyet_est <- estimate_interactions(niboyet_fit, null_models = suggest(niboyet_fit),
                                     seed = 2025)
summary(niboyet_est)
```

```{r niboyet-orders}
e <- niboyet_est$estimates
ad <- e[e$component == "interaction" & e$null_model == "AD" & e$time != "overall", ]
months <- c("0", "5", "9", "21", "33")
# Mean deviation from AD relative to the control, by number of stressors (rows)
net <- with(ad[ad$estimand == "net", ], tapply(relative, list(order, time), mean))
round(net[, months], 2)
pure <- with(ad[ad$estimand == "pure", ], tapply(relative, list(order, time), mean))
round(pure[, months], 2)
# Soil water content (%)
round(with(niboyet_denitrification, tapply(soil_water, months, mean, na.rm = TRUE)), 1)
```

```{r niboyet-numbers, include = FALSE}
smallest <- round(min(e$p_adjusted[e$component == "interaction"], na.rm = TRUE), 2)
```

No single interaction deviates from any null model once its p-value is
adjusted across the 26 sets and five samplings (the smallest adjusted
p-value is `r smallest`). The estimates, however, show the pattern of the
article. Averaged over the sets of each size, the net deviation from AD,
as a share of the control activity, is negative right after the fire and
at 21 months, the two driest samplings, positive at 5, 9 and 33 months, and
in general larger the more stressors are combined. The pure interactions
behave differently: their means change sign from one order to the next at
every sampling. The net deviation of a set of stressors adds up the pure
interactions of all its subsets of two or more stressors, 26 for five
stressors, so it grows with the number of stressors even when the pure
interactions alternate in sign, as they do here. That is what must's
distinction between net and pure interactions adds to the observation of
the article. The set of all five stressors follows the averages: below the
additive expectation right after the fire and at 21 months, above it at 5,
9 and 33 months.

```{r niboyet-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 7}
plot(niboyet_est, type = "time", set_id = unique(e$set_id[e$order == 5L]))
```

## What the case studies show

* **The design decides the replication.** `describe_design()` found the
  complete blocks of three experiments, the shared reference cells of the
  two orders, and the whole units of two: the plots of the Jasper Ridge
  experiment and the header tanks of the stream mesocosms, which replicate
  temperature and CO2 twice and not 32 times.
* **Few interactions survive with few units.** With the small-sample
  correction and p-values adjusted across sets and samplings, the plots of
  the two field experiments, the ponds and the stream mesocosms gave no
  significant interaction, where the original analyses reported some. The
  diatoms and the embryos, with large effects or many replicates, gave
  clear ones.
* **The null model decides some interactions.** When a stressor alone has a
  large effect, as continuous light on the temperate diatom, additive and
  multiplicative expectations differ enough for an observation to fall
  between them.
* **Zeros are informative, up to a point.** A combination with no embryo
  developed is tested from the probability of that outcome; a stressor
  alone with only zeros leaves its interactions not estimable.
* **Net is not pure.** With five stressors, net deviations grow with the
  number of stressors combined because they accumulate lower-order
  interactions, while the pure interactions alternate in sign.
